s0101.literal: At that time the government army's food was exhausted and all wished to withdraw; Wenyu would not allow it.
s0101.idiomatic: Government grain was gone and every man wanted to pull back. Wenyu would not hear of it.

s0102.literal: He then sent a man by hidden paths with a letter to Zhou Di, proposing brotherhood and setting out gain and harm.
s0102.idiomatic: He sent a man by hidden paths with a letter to Zhou Di, calling him brother and weighing gain against harm.

s0103.literal: Di was greatly pleased on receiving the letter and promised to send grain.
s0103.idiomatic: Di was delighted by the letter and promised grain.

s0104.literal: Thereupon Wenyu sent the old and weak down the old boats along the stream together, burned the palisade the Yuzhang commandery had set up, and feigned retreat.
s0104.idiomatic: Wenyu then sent the old and weak downriver on the old boats, burned the Yuzhang palisade, and pretended to retreat.

s0105.literal: Xiaoding watched them and was greatly pleased and therefore made no preparations.
s0105.idiomatic: Xiaoding saw them go and rejoiced, and set no guard.

s0106.literal: Wenyu by a bypath marched day and night; in two nights he reached Qianshao.
s0106.idiomatic: Wenyu took a hidden road and marched day and night; in two nights he reached Qianshao.

s0107.literal: Upstream at Qianshao were Ouyang Yi and Xiao Bo; downstream Fu Tai and Yu Xiaoding; Wenyu held the middle, built a fort, and feasted his soldiers; the rebels were greatly shaken.
s0107.idiomatic: Above Qianshao stood Ouyang Yi and Xiao Bo; below, Fu Tai and Yu Xiaoding. Wenyu held the middle, walled his men, and feasted them. The rebels were shaken.

s0108.literal: Ouyang Yi then withdrew into Nixi, built a fort, and held himself there.
s0108.idiomatic: Ouyang Yi drew into Nixi, walled himself, and held firm.

s0109.literal: Wenyu sent Stern Prestige General Zhou Tiewu, Editorial footnote marker 12. with Chief Clerk Lu Shancai to strike Yi and took him prisoner.
s0109.idiomatic: Wenyu sent Stern Prestige General Zhou Tiewu [12] and chief clerk Lu Shancai against Yi and took him.

s0110.literal: Thereupon he displayed arms in force, feasted with Yi on a boat, and cruised below Fu Tai's walls, then attacked Tai and took him.
s0110.idiomatic: He arrayed his arms, feasted with Yi on the water, and cruised under Fu Tai's walls, then stormed Tai and took him.

s0111.literal: Xiao Bo at Nankang heard of it; the troops all trembled in their thighs and none could hold firm.
s0111.idiomatic: Bo at Nankang heard the news. His troops' thighs shook; none could stand firm.

s0112.literal: His general Tan Shiyuan beheaded Bo intending to surrender but was killed by someone.
s0112.idiomatic: His general Tan Shiyuan struck off Bo's head to yield and was himself killed.

s0113.literal: Shiyuan's commander Xia Hou Mingche brought Bo's head to surrender.
s0113.idiomatic: Shiyuan's officer Xia Hou Mingche came in with Bo's head.

s0114.literal: Xiao Zi and Yu Xiaoding still held Shitou; the Founder sent Hou Andu to aid Wenyu in attacking them; Zi surrendered to Wenyu, Xiaoding fled to Xinwu, Guangzhou was pacified, and Wenyu returned to encamp at Yuzhang.
s0114.idiomatic: Xiao Zi and Yu Xiaoding still held Shitou. The Founder sent Hou Andu to help Wenyu. Zi yielded to Wenyu; Xiaoding fled to Xinwu; Guangzhou was pacified; Wenyu returned to Yuzhang.

s0115.literal: For merit he was made general who garrisons the south, opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes, commander-in-chief of the military affairs of Jiang, Guang, Heng, Jiao, and other provinces, and inspector of Jiangzhou.
s0115.idiomatic: For merit he was made general who garrisons the south with a mansion equal to the three dukes, commander-in-chief over Jiang, Guang, Heng, Jiao, and other provinces, and inspector of Jiangzhou.

s0116.literal: Wang Lin held the upper reaches; an edict appointed Hou Andu western-route commander-in-chief and Wenyu southern-route commander-in-chief to meet at Wuchang.
s0116.idiomatic: Wang Lin held the upper river. An edict made Hou Andu western commander and Wenyu southern commander to join at Wuchang.

s0117.literal: He fought Wang Lin at Dankou, was seized by Lin, and later escaped and returned—the account is in Andu's biography.
s0117.idiomatic: At Dankou he fought Wang Lin, was taken, and later escaped—the tale is in Andu's biography.

s0118.literal: Soon he was granted credential staff, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, general who garrisons the south, opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes, Duke of Shouchang, and one set of pipes and drums.
s0118.idiomatic: Soon he received credential staff, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, general who garrisons the south, opener equal to the three dukes, Duke of Shouchang, and pipes and drums.

s0119.literal: When Zhou Di broke Yu Xiaoding, Xiaoding's son Gongyang and younger brother Xiaoxun still held the old palisades and stirred the southern lands; the Founder again sent Wenyu with Zhou Di, Huang Fading, and others to campaign against them.
s0119.idiomatic: When Zhou Di broke Yu Xiaoding, Gongyang and Xiaoxun still held the old forts and stirred the south. The Founder again sent Wenyu with Zhou Di and Huang Fading against them.

s0120.literal: Xiong Tanlang, interior administrator of Yuzhang, also led troops to join them; troops numbered nearly ten thousand.
s0120.idiomatic: Xiong Tanlang, interior administrator of Yuzhang, brought his host as well; troops neared ten thousand.

s0121.literal: Wenyu made Wu Mingche the river army, assigned Zhou Di to transport grain, and himself led the army into Xiangya River and walled at Jinkou.
s0121.idiomatic: Wenyu set Wu Mingche over the fleet, Zhou Di over grain, and himself led the army up Xiangya River and fortified Jinkou.

s0122.literal: Gongyang led five hundred men in false surrender, plotting to seize Wenyu; the plot was discovered; Wenyu imprisoned him and sent him to the capital, and divided his followers among the army.
s0122.idiomatic: Gongyang came in with five hundred men in false surrender, meaning to seize Wenyu. The plot came out. Wenyu jailed him, sent him to the capital, and split his men among the loyal ranks.

s0123.literal: He then abandoned the boats for foot soldiers and advanced to hold Sanpo.
s0123.idiomatic: He left the boats for foot soldiers and advanced to Sanpo.

s0124.literal: Wang Lin sent his general Cao Qing with two thousand men to rescue Xiaoxun; Qing separately sent his commander Chang Ai to resist Wenyu and himself led his command straight against Zhou Di and Wu Mingche's army.
s0124.idiomatic: Wang Lin sent Cao Qing with two thousand men to save Xiaoxun. Qing sent Chang Ai against Wenyu and led his own command straight at Zhou Di and Wu Mingche.

s0125.literal: Di and the others were beaten; Wenyu withdrew to hold Jinkou.
s0125.idiomatic: Di and Mingche were beaten. Wenyu fell back to Jinkou.

s0126.literal: Xiong Tanlang, taking advantage of his setback, plotted to kill Wenyu to join Chang Ai.
s0126.idiomatic: Xiong Tanlang, seeing his loss, plotted to kill Wenyu and join Chang Ai.

s0127.literal: Wenyu's supervising officer Sun Baixiang knew something of the matter and urged him to strike first.
s0127.idiomatic: Wenyu's supervisor Sun Baixiang knew the plot and urged a first blow.

s0128.literal: Wenyu said: "It cannot be done. My old soldiers are few and the guest armies many; if we seize Tanlang, every man will be terrified and destruction will come at once—it is better to treat him with open heart and reassure him."
s0128.idiomatic: Wenyu said, "No. My veterans are few and allied troops many. Seize Tanlang and every man panics—ruin comes at once. Better win him with an open hand."

s0129.literal: Earlier, when Zhou Di had been beaten he abandoned his boats and fled, and no one knew where he was; when he received Di's letter Wenyu rejoiced and showed it to Tanlang; Tanlang killed him at the seat; he was fifty-one.
s0129.idiomatic: When Zhou Di had been beaten he abandoned his boats and vanished. A letter from Di came; Wenyu rejoiced and showed Tanlang. Tanlang killed him at table. He was fifty-one.

s0130.literal: When the Founder heard he mourned the same day, posthumously made him palace attendant and minister of works, and gave the posthumous title Loyal Lament.
s0130.idiomatic: The Founder mourned the same day, posthumously made him palace attendant and minister of works, and titled him Loyal Lament.

s0131.literal: Earlier, when Wenyu held Sanpo, a shooting star fell to earth with a sound like thunder; the ground sank one zhang square and held several dou of broken charcoal.
s0131.idiomatic: When Wenyu held Sanpo a meteor fell with thunder. The earth sank a square zhang and held several dou of charred coal.

s0132.literal: Again in the army market a child's cry was suddenly heard; the whole market was alarmed; listening, it was under the earth; soldiers dug and found a coffin three chi long; Wenyu hated the omen.
s0132.idiomatic: In the army market a child seemed to cry under the ground. Soldiers dug up a coffin three chi long. Wenyu hated the sign.

s0133.literal: Before long Di was beaten and Wenyu was killed.
s0133.idiomatic: Soon Di was beaten and Wenyu was slain.

s0134.literal: In the second year of Tiancheng an edict ordered him to share offerings in the Founder's temple hall.
s0134.idiomatic: In Tiancheng year 2 (561) an edict gave him shared sacrifice in the Founder's temple.

s0136.literal: Wenyu's clansman Jingyao, through Wenyu, reached the post of administrator of Xin'an.
s0136.idiomatic: Wenyu's kinsman Jingyao, through Wenyu's favor, became administrator of Xin'an.

s0138.literal: In his teens he was already skilled in riding and archery; as a noble's son he was proud, dissolute, and fond of roaming; he loved dogs and horses, delighted in the gallop, dressed in splendor and ate in idleness.
s0138.idiomatic: In his teens he rode and shot well. As a noble's son he was proud and wild, loved hounds and horses, dressed fine, and ate idle.

s0139.literal: When Wenyu was at Jinling, because campaigns left no leisure for the commandery he had Bao'an oversee commandery affairs; he especially gathered wicked youths; the Founder was troubled by it.
s0139.idiomatic: When Wenyu held Jinling he left Bao'an to run the commandery while he fought, and the boy gathered rowdies. The Founder disliked it.

s0140.literal: When Wenyu was beaten on the western campaign and held by Wang Lin, Bao'an at once reformed himself, read books, kept company with gentlemen, and pacified Wenyu's soldiers with great authority and kindness.
s0140.idiomatic: When Wenyu was beaten west and held by Wang Lin, Bao'an turned sober, read books, kept gentlemen's company, and ruled Wenyu's soldiers with stern kindness.

s0141.literal: He was made supernumerary scattered-cavalry gentleman.
s0141.idiomatic: He was made supernumerary scattered-cavalry gentleman.

s0142.literal: When Wenyu returned he was again made steadfast-prestige general and administrator of Wuxing.
s0142.idiomatic: When Wenyu came home he was again made steadfast-prestige general and administrator of Wuxing.

s0143.literal: When Wenyu was killed by Xiong Tanlang, Bao'an was recalled.
s0143.idiomatic: When Xiong Tanlang killed Wenyu, Bao'an was recalled.

s0144.literal: He was raised to fierce martial general, given command of his father's old troops, and still ordered south on campaign.
s0144.idiomatic: He was made fierce-martial general, given his father's old troops, and sent south again.

s0145.literal: When Emperor Wen succeeded to the throne he valued him deeply, entrusted him as a confidant, and gave him many picked soldiers and sharp weapons.
s0145.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen took the throne he prized him, kept him close, and gave him picked men and good arms.

s0146.literal: When Wang Lin was pacified he had considerable merit.
s0146.idiomatic: In pacifying Wang Lin he won solid merit.

s0147.literal: When Zhou Di broke Xiong Tanlang, Bao'an marched south and hunted down the last embers.
s0147.idiomatic: When Zhou Di broke Xiong Tanlang, Bao'an marched south and stamped out the last embers.

s0148.literal: In the second year of Tiancheng he was again made stern-faith general and administrator of Wuxing and succeeded to the enfeoffment as Duke of Shouchang.
s0148.idiomatic: In Tiancheng year 2 (561) he was again stern-faith general and administrator of Wuxing and succeeded as Duke of Shouchang.

s0149.literal: In the third year he campaigned against Liu Yi and was Hou Andu's vanguard.
s0149.idiomatic: In year 3 he campaigned against Liu Yi as Hou Andu's vanguard.

s0150.literal: When Yi was pacified he was made gentleman of the yellow gate and commandant of the guard.
s0150.idiomatic: When Yi fell he was made gentleman of the yellow gate and commandant of the guard.

s0151.literal: In the fourth year he was granted credential staff, made commander-in-chief of the military affairs of South Xuzhou, steadfast-resolve general, and inspector of South Xuzhou.
s0151.idiomatic: In year 4 he received credential staff, command over South Xuzhou, steadfast-resolve general, and inspector of South Xuzhou.

s0152.literal: He was recalled and made left guard general and given the additional title faithful-martial general.
s0152.idiomatic: Recalled, he was made left guard general with the added title faithful-martial general.

s0153.literal: Soon, retaining his former office, he also headed the guard commandant's office and was advanced in title to benevolent-prestige general.
s0153.idiomatic: Soon he also headed the guard while keeping his rank, and was raised to benevolent-prestige general.

s0154.literal: In the first year of Tiankang he died, aged twenty-nine.
s0154.idiomatic: In Tiankang year 1 (566) he died, aged twenty-nine.

s0155.literal: He was posthumously made palace attendant and left guard general, with the posthumous title Accomplished.
s0155.idiomatic: Posthumously he was palace attendant and left guard general, titled Accomplished.

s0157.literal: After Bao'an died Ke also served as a subordinate general.
s0157.idiomatic: After Bao'an died Ke too served as a subordinate general.

s0158.literal: Campaigning against Ouyang He and pacifying Huainan he had merit, was enfeoffed as Earl of Jiang'an with a fief of four hundred households.
s0158.idiomatic: On campaign against Ouyang He and in pacifying Huainan he won merit and was enfeoffed Earl of Jiang'an with four hundred households.

s0159.literal: He served as administrator of Jinling and Dingyuan commanderies.
s0159.idiomatic: He was administrator of Jinling and Dingyuan.

s0160.literal: In the ninth year of Taijian he died, aged twenty-four, and was posthumously made serene-prestige general.
s0160.idiomatic: In Taijian year 9 (581) he died, aged twenty-four, and was posthumously made serene-prestige general.

s0161.literal: Hou Andu, style Chengshi, was a native of Qujiang in Shixing.
s0161.idiomatic: Hou Andu, styled Chengshi, came from Qujiang in Shixing.

s0162.literal: For generations his house was a leading clan of the commandery.
s0162.idiomatic: For generations his house was a leading clan in the commandery.

s0163.literal: His father Wenhan, Editorial footnote marker 13. in youth served in the province and commandery and was known for loyalty and care; after Andu rose high he reached the posts of grand master for the imperial insignia and interior administrator of Shixing, with salary of middle two thousand dan.
s0163.idiomatic: His father Wenhan [13] served the province and commandery in youth and was known for loyalty. After Andu rose, Wenhan became grand master for the imperial insignia and interior administrator of Shixing at middle two-thousand-dan rank.

s0164.literal: Andu was skilled in clerical script, could play the zither, ranged through books and records, composed five-character poems that were also rather refined, and was besides skilled in riding and archery—a local hero.
s0164.idiomatic: Andu wrote clerical script, played the zither, read widely, wrote five-character verse of some grace, rode and shot well, and was a hero in his district.

s0165.literal: Xiao Zifan, interior administrator of Shixing under Liang, summoned him as chief clerk.
s0165.idiomatic: Under Liang, Xiao Zifan, interior administrator of Shixing, took him as chief clerk.

s0166.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion he gathered arms and armor to three thousand men.
s0166.idiomatic: In Hou Jing's rebellion he gathered arms for three thousand men.

s0167.literal: When the Founder entered to relieve the capital region, Andu led troops to follow the Founder, attacked Cai Luyang, broke Li Qianshi, and in conquering and pacifying Hou Jing fought with all his strength and had merit.
s0167.idiomatic: When the Founder marched to relieve the capital, Andu followed with troops, struck Cai Luyang, broke Li Qianshi, and in crushing Hou Jing fought with all his might and won honor.

s0168.literal: Emperor Yuan granted him fierce-martial general, direct-communication scattered-cavalry regular attendant, and enfeoffment as Viscount of Fuchuan with a fief of three hundred households.
s0168.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan of Liang made him fierce-martial general and direct-communication scattered-cavalry regular attendant, and Viscount of Fuchuan with three hundred households.

s0169.literal: He followed the Founder in garrison at Jingkou and was made administrator of Lanling.
s0169.idiomatic: He followed the Founder to Jingkou and was made administrator of Lanling.

s0170.literal: When the Founder plotted to strike Wang Sengbian none of the generals knew; he alone settled the plan with Andu and still had Andu lead the river army from Jingkou toward Shitou while the Founder himself led horse and foot from Jiangcheng and Luoluo to join him.
s0170.idiomatic: When the Founder plotted against Wang Sengbian no general knew but Andu. Andu led the river force from Jingkou on Shitou while the Founder came with horse and foot from Jiangcheng and Luoluo to meet him.

s0171.literal: Andu reached the north of Shitou, abandoned his boats, and went ashore; Sengbian did not perceive him.
s0171.idiomatic: Andu reached north Shitou, left his boats, and went ashore unseen by Sengbian.

s0172.literal: Shitou's north adjoins hills; the parapet was not very steep; Andu wore armor and carried a long blade; soldiers lifted him and cast him over the inner parapet; troops followed within, pressed forward, and closed on Sengbian's sleeping chamber.
s0172.idiomatic: North Shitou runs into hills and the wall was low. Andu wore armor and a long blade; soldiers lifted him onto the inner parapet; troops poured in and pressed on Sengbian's chamber.

s0173.literal: The Founder's great army also arrived and fought Sengbian before the audience hall; Andu came out from the inner quarters and struck front and rear; he took Sengbian prisoner.
s0173.idiomatic: The Founder's host came up and fought Sengbian before the hall. Andu burst from the inner quarters and struck fore and aft. Sengbian was taken.

s0174.literal: The next spring an edict ordered Andu to lead troops to garrison Liang Mountain against Qi.
s0174.idiomatic: Next spring an edict set Andu to garrison Liang Mountain against Qi.

s0175.literal: Xu Siwei and others again entered Danyang, Editorial footnote marker 14. reaching Hushu; the Founder recalled Andu and led horse and foot to resist them at Gaoqiao.
s0175.idiomatic: Xu Siwei again entered Danyang [14] as far as Hushu. The Founder recalled Andu and met them at Gaoqiao with horse and foot.

s0176.literal: Again they fought south of Gengtan; Andu led twelve horsemen and burst their line, broke them, and took alive Qi Acting Minister of State Qifu Wulao.
s0176.idiomatic: They fought again south of Gengtan. Andu with twelve riders burst the line, broke them, and took Qifu Wulao of Qi alive.

s0177.literal: He also speared Qi general Dongfang Lao and knocked him from his horse; rebel horsemen came and rescued Lao, who escaped.
s0177.idiomatic: He speared Qi general Dongfang Lao from the saddle; enemy riders came and Lao escaped.

s0178.literal: The bandits crossed north over Jiangshan; Andu again fought Qi general Wang Jingbao at Longwei and sent his cousin Xiao and commander Zhang Zuan to strike the front of their line.
s0178.idiomatic: The rebels crossed Jiangshan north. Andu fought Wang Jingbao of Qi at Longwei and sent his cousin Xiao and Zhang Zuan against the van.

s0179.literal: Xiao was speared and fell from his horse; Zhang Zuan died in the fight.
s0179.idiomatic: Xiao took a spear and fell. Zhang Zuan died on the field.

s0180.literal: Andu galloped to save Xiao, beheaded eleven of their horsemen, took Zuan's corpse and returned, and the Qi army did not dare press him.
s0180.idiomatic: Andu galloped to Xiao, killed eleven horsemen, bore Zuan's body back, and Qi did not dare follow.

s0181.literal: The Founder fought the Qi army at Mofu Mountain and ordered Andu to lead more than a thousand foot and horse from Baixia to strike them in the rear crosswise; the Qi army was routed utterly.
s0181.idiomatic: At Mofu Mountain the Founder fought Qi and sent Andu with more than a thousand horse and foot from Baixia to strike their rear. Qi broke utterly.

s0182.literal: Editorial footnote marker 15. Andu again led his command in pursuit to She Mountain, capturing heads and prisoners beyond counting.
s0182.idiomatic: [15] Andu pursued to She Mountain and took heads and prisoners past counting.

s0183.literal: For merit he was advanced in enfeoffment to marquis, his fief increased by five hundred households, and he was given one set of pipes and drums.
s0183.idiomatic: For merit his fief was raised to marquis with five hundred added households and he received pipes and drums.

s0184.literal: He was again advanced in title to general who pacifies the south and his enfeoffment changed to Duke of Xijiang.
s0184.idiomatic: He was raised to general who pacifies the south and made Duke of Xijiang.

s0185.literal: He still commanded the river army out of Yuzhang to aid Inspector of Yuzhou Zhou Wenyu in campaigning against Xiao Bo.
s0185.idiomatic: He still commanded the fleet from Yuzhang to aid Zhou Wenyu, inspector of Yuzhou, against Xiao Bo.

s0186.literal: Andu had not yet arrived when Wenyu had already beheaded Bo and also taken his generals Ouyang Yi, Fu Tai, and others prisoner.
s0186.idiomatic: Before Andu arrived Wenyu had beheaded Bo and taken Ouyang Yi, Fu Tai, and others.

s0187.literal: Only Yu Xiaoding and Bo's son Zi still held Shitou in Yuzhang, building two cities; Xiaoding and Zi each held one; they also set out many ships and boats and lined their battle line across the water.
s0187.idiomatic: Only Yu Xiaoding and Bo's son Zi still held Shitou in Yuzhang in twin cities. They massed ships and lined the water with battle line.

s0188.literal: When Andu arrived he had men take sticks in their mouths by night and burn their ships.
s0188.idiomatic: Andu came, had men gag themselves with sticks at night, and burned their fleet.

s0189.literal: Wenyu led the river army; Andu led foot and horse; they went ashore and formed battle lines.
s0189.idiomatic: Wenyu led the fleet; Andu the foot and horse. They landed and formed line.

s0190.literal: Xiaoding soon cut off the rear road; Andu then ordered the soldiers to cut much pine wood, pile palisades, advance camp by camp, fought repeatedly and won repeatedly, and Zi then surrendered.
s0190.idiomatic: Xiaoding cut the retreat. Andu had pine felled, palisades raised, camps pushed forward, won fight after fight, and Zi yielded.

s0191.literal: Xiaoding fled back to Xinwu and asked to send his son as hostage; this was permitted.
s0191.idiomatic: Xiaoding fled to Xinwu and offered his son as hostage; the court agreed.

s0192.literal: When the army returned, for merit he was advanced in title to general who garrisons the north and given opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes.
s0192.idiomatic: On return he was raised to general who garrisons the north and opener equal to the three dukes.

s0193.literal: He still led the army to join at Wuchang with Zhou Wenyu in the western campaign against Wang Lin.
s0193.idiomatic: He still led troops to Wuchang to join Zhou Wenyu against Wang Lin in the west.

s0194.literal: As they were about to set out, from the nobles down they saw them off at Xinlin; Andu leaped his horse over a bridge, man and horse both falling into the water; again, sitting in a skiff he fell into the sculling-well in the cabin—at the time it was thought ill-omened.
s0194.idiomatic: At Xinlin nobles saw them off. Andu leaped a bridge and horse and rider plunged into the water; in a skiff he fell into the sculling-well—omens of ill luck.

s0195.literal: Reaching Wuchang, Wang Lin's general Fan Meng abandoned the city and fled.
s0195.idiomatic: At Wuchang Wang Lin's general Fan Meng abandoned the city and fled.

s0197.literal: At that time both generals marched together without unified command; because their subordinates quarreled they grew somewhat estranged.
s0197.idiomatic: Both generals marched without one command. Their men quarreled and the two grew cool.

s0198.literal: The army reached Yingzhou; Wang Lin's general Pan Chunzhi shot at the government army from the city from afar; Editorial footnote marker 16. Andu was enraged, advanced and besieged the city, but could not take it.
s0198.idiomatic: At Yingzhou Wang Lin's general Pan Chunzhi shot from the walls. [16] Andu raged, besieged the city, and could not take it.

s0199.literal: Wang Lin then reached Yan mouth; Andu released Yingzhou and led all the troops to Dankou to meet him but met wind and could not advance.
s0199.idiomatic: Wang Lin reached Yan mouth. Andu left Yingzhou, marched every man to Dankou, and was stopped by wind.

s0200.literal: Lin held the east bank and the government army the west; they faced each other several days, then joined battle; Andu and the others were beaten.
s0200.idiomatic: Lin held the east bank, the loyal army the west. After days they fought. Andu and the rest were beaten.
